analysis.one_liner: Requires for-profit colleges to earn more revenue outside federal aid and counts GI Bill benefits as federal money.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action in two years; it died with 54 cosponsors when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law says for-profit colleges must get at least 10% of their revenue from non-federal sources before they can hand out federal student aid. This bill would double that to 20% and, crucially, start counting GI Bill education benefits as federal money. That closes what critics called the "90/10 loophole," where for-profit schools could rely almost entirely on federal dollars — including veterans' benefits — because GI Bill money wasn't counted.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers and veterans. Veterans in particular would gain, because schools could no longer chase their GI Bill dollars without limit — under current law, a for-profit school could draw 90% of its revenue from federal student aid plus unlimited GI Bill money and still qualify for aid programs. The bill would also force the Education Department to publish each for-profit school's share of federal revenue annually [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the non-federal revenue requirement for for-profit colleges from 10% to 20%, so a school must draw a real share of its income from tuition paid outside federal aid to keep access to federal student aid programs.

Counts GI Bill education benefits as federal funds — with an exception for the Post-9/11 monthly housing stipend — closing the loophole that let schools target veterans' benefits as if they were private revenue.

Tightens how revenue is counted: institutional scholarships only count if funded from an outside source with no ties to the school, refunded federal money doesn't count, and Federal Work-Study funds are excluded, making it harder to game the ratio with affiliated scholarships.

Requires the Education Secretary to report to Congress every year, for each for-profit school receiving federal aid, exactly how much of its revenue comes from federal education funds — making each school's dependence on taxpayers public.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies and their investors. Schools that cannot get 20% of revenue from non-federal sources lose eligibility for federal student aid entirely, which for many would mean losing most of their customers and revenue. Some would shrink; some would close.

drawbacks.text: A school that fails the 20% test loses access to all federal student aid, not just a portion of it — the bill has no partial penalty — so schools near the line could close abruptly or stop enrolling federal-aid and GI Bill students, disrupting students mid-program.

The rules for counting revenue are detailed and accounting-heavy, and schools would bear the cost of audits and compliance; some schools serving nontraditional students with few other payment options would face the hardest adjustment, even if they enroll students in good faith.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real: under current law a for-profit school can be almost entirely federally funded — with GI Bill dollars not even counting toward the limit — and there is no annual public accounting of how dependent each school is [S2][S3]. The main cost is disruption for students enrolled at schools that cannot adjust within the one-year lead time the bill allows [S3]. A stronger version would phase in the 20% threshold over several years; as written, the tradeoff is a hard cliff in exchange for closing a loophole that puts veterans' benefits squarely in the crosshairs of aggressive recruiting.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Donna Shalala introduced the bill on June 19, 2019, joined by seven original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor — the only action the bill ever received.
Over the following months it accumulated 54 cosponsors, 53 Democrats and 1 Republican, but the committee never scheduled a markup or vote.
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021, so the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges and their investors are better off: the 10% rule stays in place and GI Bill benefits still don't count as federal revenue, so schools can keep recruiting veterans' tuition dollars without limit. Veterans and student borrowers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Donna Shalala
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to double the non-federal revenue requirement and count GI Bill benefits as federal funds.

for.name: Veterans service organizations
for.what_they_did: Pushed for years to close the 90/10 loophole that lets for-profit schools count veterans' GI Bill benefits as non-federal revenue.

against.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; it sat with no action after referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.role: Industry lobby (trade group Career Education Colleges and Universities)
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against changes to the 90/10 rule and counting GI Bill benefits as federal revenue.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call to measure; its 54 cosponsors were 53 Democrats and 1 Republican, so support skewed heavily Democratic.

industries.note: These schools live on federal money: current law only requires 10% of revenue from non-federal sources, and GI Bill benefits don't count as federal at all. The bill doubles the requirement and counts veterans' benefits as federal funds, so any school that can't find a fifth of its revenue outside federal aid loses access to federal student aid — its main customer base [S2][S3].
